extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers interested in moral philosophy and Renaissance essays
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for composing and reasoning in personal moral/philosophical essays in the style of Montaigne: virtues, rhetorical stances, and educational commentary. Emphasises judgment, practical wisdom, and candid illustrative examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer clemency and forgiveness over revenge
rubrics_metrics.description: When in doubt between punishment and pardon, choose that course which has the greatest appearance of honesty and justice; it is more noble and generous to pardon than to avenge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne illustrates with Augustus forgiving Cinna (making him a friend and later consul) and contrasts occasional ill outcomes (the Duke de Guise) but argues the intention and nobility of clemency remain praiseworthy. The text advises choosing the action that appears more honorable rather than the most expedient or safest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge Fortune’s decisive role in success
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that chance or Fortune has a great part in all arts and enterprises; successes often exceed the practitioner's sufficiency and are partly due to luck.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: poets and painters experience raptures or strokes of genius beyond their conscious control; military exploits often rely on Fortune despite counsel. Anti-pattern: crediting skill alone and ignoring chance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose the noblest course over the shortest/safest
rubrics_metrics.description: In uncertainty, adopt the action that shows the greatest appearance of honesty and justice rather than merely the most direct or safe path.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne argues that because human wisdom is shortsighted and circumstances unpredictable, moral appearance and nobility should guide action. Example: pardoning an offender may be the nobler choice even if it risks personal harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive suspicion and over-circumspection
rubrics_metrics.description: Overly wary prudence and continual suspicion are enemies of great and generous exploits; excessive jealousy of friends and constant guard lead to torment and ruin of spirit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited examples: Dion’s refusal to live under perpetual fear, Alexander drinking the potion to show confidence. Practical guidance: while vigilance has utility, living in constant distrust is harmful and undermines action and dignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Display confident, undaunted assurance when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Courage is effectively conveyed by a composed and fearless countenance; genuine resolution must be embodied, not merely pretended with fearfulness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A public, confident demeanor can win hearts or quell mutiny (e.g., Caesar facing mutinous legions). Anti-pattern: feigning confidence while visibly trembling defeats the purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary submission can build reciprocal trust
rubrics_metrics.description: Submitting oneself freely and seemingly without constraint to another's mercy or good will is an effective method to gain their heart and repose confidence in them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The submission must appear freely given, not forced; examples include rulers putting themselves into enemies’ hands to demonstrate trust and elicit reciprocal trust. Beware of naive self-endangerment without dignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish intelligence to deter conspirators
rubrics_metrics.description: Princes should publicly disclose the informations they receive about plots against them to create an impression of omniscience and thus keep enemies in awe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Dionysius counting out money to a braggart who claimed to know how to discover conspiracies—using the claim itself as deterrence. Use disclosure strategically to project control; anti-pattern: secret hoarding of intelligence that fails to deter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept unavoidable danger rather than live in perpetual fear
rubrics_metrics.description: When remedies for a danger only produce anxiety and uncertainty, it may be better to prepare for the worst and accept it than to endure continual dread and evasive life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anecdote: a Roman at large voluntarily surrendered to end perpetual fleeing. Practical advice: consider the quality of life under perpetual fear vs. measured acceptance of risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education should cultivate judgment and virtue, not only memory
rubrics_metrics.description: True education aims to make students better in judgment and character, not merely to fill their heads with facts and quotations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne criticizes parental investment that only furnishes the head; he insists on forming conscience and understanding. Anti-pattern: praising someone merely for knowing Greek/Latin while ignoring their moral disposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value being better learned over being more learned
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess learners by the quality and applicability of their understanding ('better learned'), not by the sheer quantity of their erudition ('more learned').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer practical wisdom and discretion to an accumulation of citations. Example guidance: enquire whether study made one wiser, not merely more pedantically informed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make knowledge your own — internalize and digest it
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not merely collect and repeat others' sayings; integrate learning into your own judgment so it nourishes and supports you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metaphor: food that isn't digested is useless; knowledge should be assimilated. Anti-patterns: parroting citations, borrowing consolation wholesale from Seneca or Cicero rather than reasoning oneself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pedantry: do not display knowledge without understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Pedantry consists in ostentatious, superficial learning that lacks judgment; pedants speak learnedly but do not improve matters and often make things worse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characteristics: stuffed memory, empty judgment, dependence on prompting, using high-flown or obsolete language to impress. Examples: university-trained men who are useless in practical affairs. Remedies: cultivate common sense and practical competence alongside learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer applied learning and practical exercises
rubrics_metrics.description: If learning does not improve disposition or judgment, physical or practical exercises (e.g., tennis) may be preferable to formal study that leaves one unfit for action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne suggests that a scholar whose study leaves him useless would have been better served by bodily or practical pursuits that develop other faculties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not take others' opinions on blind trust — think critically
rubrics_metrics.description: Relying on other people's knowledge 'on trust' produces idle and superficial learning; one must examine, appropriate, and reason about sources oneself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: men who call for books to answer even trivial questions. Guidance: question authorities, develop independent reasoning, and avoid becoming a mere repository of quotations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of letting study crowd out practical capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive accumulation of learned matter should not constrict the active part of understanding or make one incapable of practical employment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne rejects the notion that adding many foreign conceptions necessarily reduces native capacity, yet warns that the way study is pursued can leave one swollen with useless scraps rather than useful judgment. Remedy: balance study with practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educators should be accountable for practical benefit
rubrics_metrics.description: Teachers and pedagogues who claim usefulness should be judged by whether their instruction yields real advantage to their pupils, not merely by scholarly reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne references Protagoras’ rule (pay by value received) as an ideal test. Anti-pattern: tutors who leave pupils learned but not wise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid elevating erudition as social capital over goodness
rubrics_metrics.description: Society often admires the learned more than the good; this is a misvaluation — learning without moral improvement is a defect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe social criers praising learned men while neglecting to hail morally good men. Practical advice: prioritize moral development when evaluating persons.
